## Overview

Express is a minimal, unopinionated HTTP application framework for Node.js. An
application is a stack of middleware functions and routes mounted on an `app` object;
each incoming request is decorated into an Express `req` and each outgoing response into
an Express `res`, and the two prototypes in `lib/request.js` and `lib/response.js` are
where nearly all of the framework's observable behavior lives. `lib/application.js`
carries the app object itself — `app.set`, the setting compilers, and the routing entry
points — and `lib/utils.js` holds the shared helpers those two layers call into:
media-type parsing, ETag/query-parser/trust-proxy compilation, and charset injection.

The people this specification serves are application developers who call the `res.*`
response helpers and read the `req.*` derived getters, and the operators who deploy those
applications behind reverse proxies. Data flows one way: a raw Node `IncomingMessage`
arrives, `req` getters re-derive user-meaningful values (scheme, host, hostname,
subdomains, negotiated content type) from headers, application code decides what to send,
and the `res` helpers serialize that decision into status line, headers, and body. Express
v5's design philosophy is to stay thin over Node's own HTTP objects, delegating to small
focused libraries (`cookie`, `statuses`, `mime-types`, `content-type`) rather than
reimplementing them. That thinness is exactly where this derivation concentrated: the
seams where Express hand-rolls parsing or hand-composes a header, and the places where two
code paths that a developer would expect to agree were written independently.

The requirements below are all derived from reading `lib/*.js` directly. Evidence base:
the Express v5.2.1 source tree, the gathered Tier-4 documentation in `reference_docs/`,
and `History.md` as changelog context — notably the v5 entry at `History.md:15` recording
a fix to "avoid duplicate Content-Type processing in `res.send()`", which is the
documentary basis for treating charset handling as a parity surface rather than a single
path. Tier distribution is uniform: eight product REQs, all Tier 3, no Tier 1 or Tier 2
citations, because there is no external normative specification for Express itself. Two
REQs (REQ-005 and REQ-007) are multi-site parity requirements and carry a `Pattern:` tag;
they emit per-site use cases (`UC-06.a/b/c`, `UC-07.a/b/c`) so each site is exercised
independently rather than collapsing into a single representative case.

### Coverage and known gaps

This derivation is thin, and the operator should read it as thin. Eight product
requirements for an entire web framework is not coverage of Express — it is coverage of a
handful of high-yield seams in `lib/request.js`, `lib/response.js`, and `lib/utils.js`.
The following surfaces were explored or skimmed and knowingly did **not** become
requirements: the router and layer matching machinery (path-to-regexp integration, param
callbacks, mounting and `req.baseUrl`/`req.url` rewriting), `res.sendFile` and the
static/range-request path, view rendering and the template engine registry, error handling
and the default error middleware, the ETag generation strategies themselves (only their
compilation is constrained, by REQ-008), body parsing (which lives in dependencies rather
than in `lib/`), and the entire `express.Router()` public surface. Those areas were passed
over not because they are low-risk but because this run prioritized cross-implementation
consistency seams — two code paths that should agree and were written separately — over
breadth. Anything reached only through the framework's dependencies (`cookie`, `send`,
`body-parser`, `path-to-regexp`) is out of reach of this run by construction: the audit
scope is the Express source tree, and a defect inside a dependency is not an Express REQ.
Treat the sections below as a deep probe of response serialization, content negotiation,
and proxy-header derivation — not as a specification of Express.

## Actors and roles

- **Application developer** — writes route handlers and calls `res.cookie`, `res.redirect`,
  `res.jsonp`, `res.send`, `res.json`, `res.set`, and `res.type`. Needs the response
  helpers to serialize exactly what was asked for, with no self-contradicting headers and
  no leaked `undefined` in a user-visible body. This actor owns most of the requirements
  below.
- **Application operator / deployer** — runs the app behind a TLS-terminating reverse
  proxy or load balancer and configures `trust proxy`, `etag`, and `query parser` through
  `app.set`. Needs the `X-Forwarded-*` derivations to be trustworthy when trust is enabled
  and misconfiguration to surface at boot rather than under load.
- **HTTP client** — a browser or API consumer that sends `Accept` headers with quality
  values and media-type parameters, and that consumes cookies, redirects, and JSONP
  payloads. Never reads this document, but every requirement below is ultimately a promise
  made to this actor about bytes on the wire.
- **Reviewer / auditor** — reads this document to decide whether the derivation captured
  Express's intent before trusting any downstream finding. The coverage statement above is
  addressed to this actor first.

Functional sections below are ordered user-facing → infrastructure: what a developer or
client observes on the wire comes first, what the framework derives or compiles on their
behalf comes last.

## Response construction and serialization

The contract theme of this section is that every `res.*` helper which composes a header or
a body must emit a result that is internally consistent and free of serialization
artifacts. These are the most user-visible surfaces in Express: a developer calls one
method and a client receives bytes, with no opportunity to inspect or correct what was
built in between. Each requirement here constrains a single helper in `lib/response.js`
that hand-composes output from caller-supplied values, and the failure mode each guards
against is the same shape — a header or body that is syntactically well-formed but
semantically self-contradicting, so nothing downstream rejects it.

### REQ-001: `res.cookie` Max-Age and Expires directives that agree
- Tier: 3
- References: lib/response.js:742-775, lib/response.js:759-766
- Implementation: `maxAge` (ms) is converted to `expires` and floored to seconds for `Max-Age`.
- Conditions of satisfaction: a sub-second `maxAge` must not serialize `Max-Age=0` alongside a future `Expires`; `res.clearCookie` (response.js:709-716) remains the only path that sets an immediate expiry. `res.cookie` must not emit a `Max-Age` that contradicts a future `Expires`.
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-02

### REQ-002: Well-formed `res.redirect` body for any accepted status code
- Tier: 3
- References: lib/response.js:812-864
- Implementation: the body is built from `statuses.message[status]` via `res.format`.
- Conditions of satisfaction: `res.redirect` must produce a well-formed body for any status code it accepts. For a status with no `statuses.message` entry, the body and HTML `<title>` must not contain the literal string `undefined`.
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-03

### REQ-003: Safe, well-defined grammar for `res.jsonp` callback names
- Tier: 3
- References: lib/response.js:260-304, lib/response.js:286
- Implementation: the callback is filtered by `/[^\[\]\w$.]/g` then reflected into a `text/javascript` body guarded by `typeof … === 'function'`.
- Conditions of satisfaction: `res.jsonp` callback names must be restricted to a safe, well-defined grammar. Only callback strings matching the intended grammar reach the body; member-access chains either are rejected or are proven safe by the guard. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` is always set on jsonp responses (response.js:271,282).
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-04

## Content negotiation and charset consistency

The contract theme of this section is agreement about media types: what Express parses out
of a client's `Accept` header, and what it writes back into `Content-Type` on the way out.
Both requirements concern the same shared vocabulary — a `type/subtype` with parameters —
handled by code that was written independently on the inbound and outbound sides. The
inbound requirement constrains a hand-rolled parser in `lib/utils.js` that stands in for a
grammar-aware one; the outbound requirement is a parity requirement across four response
surfaces that inject charset through two different mechanisms. A reviewer should read them
together: an inconsistency here is invisible to any single code path and only appears when
two paths that describe the same media type are compared.

### REQ-004: RFC 7231 §3.1.1.1-conformant media-type parameter parsing in `acceptParams`
- Tier: 3
- References: lib/utils.js:89-120, lib/utils.js:61-77
- Implementation: hand-rolled scan over `;`/`=` boundaries extracting `q` and `params`.
- Conditions of satisfaction: `acceptParams` must parse media-type parameters per RFC 7231 §3.1.1.1. Quoted parameter values containing `;` are not split mid-value; `q` is parsed and clamped to `[0,1]`; the `splitIndex > endIndex` recovery branch (utils.js:102-104) does not drop valid params.
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-05

### REQ-005: Consistent charset handling across `res.send` body types and the `res.set`/`res.type`/`res.json`/`res.jsonp` surfaces
- Tier: 3
- Pattern: parity
- References: lib/response.js:137-143, lib/response.js:150-153, lib/response.js:664-686, lib/utils.js:225-238
- Implementation: string `send` rewrites charset to utf-8 via `setCharset`; Buffer `send` preserves it; `res.set`/`res.type` inject charset via `mime.contentType`.
- Conditions of satisfaction (per-site, see UC-06.a/b/c): charset handling must be consistent across `res.send` body types and the `res.set`/`res.type`/`res.json`/`res.jsonp` surfaces.
  - UC-06.a: a pre-set non-utf-8 charset sent as a **string** body must behave per the documented v5 rule (force utf-8) consistently.
  - UC-06.b: the same charset sent as a **Buffer** body must follow the same documented rule, or the divergence must be explicitly specified.
  - UC-06.c: `res.set('Content-Type', …)` charset injection (via `mime.contentType`) must agree with `res.send`'s `setCharset` injection for the same input.
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-06.a, UC-06.b, UC-06.c

## Trust-proxy derivation and settings compilation

The contract theme of this section is the values Express derives on the developer's behalf
from configuration and from headers it does not itself control. `lib/request.js`
re-derives `protocol`/`secure`/`host`/`hostname`/`ip`/`subdomains` from untrusted
`X-Forwarded-*` headers, gated by the trust-proxy function that `app.set` compiles; two of
those getters read two headers with the same shape (comma-separated lists) using
*different* split and trim discipline, which makes this the central
cross-implementation-consistency surface for this run. The settings requirement belongs
here rather than in a section of its own because the compiler it constrains
(`compileTrust`, alongside `compileETag` and `compileQueryParser`) is what produces the
very trust-proxy function the two header requirements depend on: a silently-accepted bad
`trust proxy` value and a mis-derived `req.protocol` are the same failure seen at two
different moments.

### REQ-006: Non-empty, correct `req.protocol` scheme for every trusted `X-Forwarded-Proto` value
- Tier: 3
- References: lib/request.js:297-315, lib/request.js:326-328
- Implementation: `req.protocol` getter comma-splits and trims the forwarded header; `req.secure` derives from it.
- Conditions of satisfaction: `req.protocol` must yield a non-empty, correct scheme for every trusted `X-Forwarded-Proto` value. For header values `""`, `","`, `", https"`, `"https,"`, `"http, https"` with trust proxy enabled, `req.protocol ∈ {http, https}` and `req.secure` reflects the real scheme.
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-01

### REQ-007: Consistent `req.host`/`req.hostname`/`req.subdomains` resolution for all trusted `X-Forwarded-Host` shapes
- Tier: 3
- Pattern: parity
- References: lib/request.js:418-431, lib/request.js:444-458, lib/request.js:383-394
- Implementation: `host` selects/trims XFH then `Host`; `hostname` strips the port; `subdomains` splits on `.`.
- Conditions of satisfaction (per-site, see UC-07.a/b/c): `req.host`/`req.hostname`/`req.subdomains` must resolve consistently for all trusted `X-Forwarded-Host` shapes. For trusted XFH values `"a.com"`, `",a.com"`, `"a.com,"`, `"a.com:8080"`, `"[::1]:8080"`, each of `host`/`hostname`/`subdomains` returns the value implied by the leading authority, never `undefined` for a syntactically present host.
- Specificity: specific
- Use cases: UC-07.a, UC-07.b, UC-07.c

### REQ-008: Fail-fast settings compilation on invalid configuration
- Tier: 3
- References: lib/application.js:363-380, lib/utils.js:130-214
- Implementation: `compileETag`/`compileQueryParser`/`compileTrust` throw `TypeError` on unknown values at `app.set` time.
- Conditions of satisfaction: settings compilation must fail fast on invalid configuration — invalid values for `etag`/`query parser`/`trust proxy` throw a `TypeError` at `app.set` time, not at request time.
- Specificity: architectural-guidance (cross-cutting config invariant, not a single testable path)

## Cross-cutting concerns

**No user-visible `undefined`.** Express composes several outputs by indexing a lookup
table with a caller-supplied value: `statuses.message[status]` in the redirect body
(REQ-002), `statuses.message` again in the default error body, `mime` lookups in
`res.type`. Wherever a lookup can miss, the miss must not reach the wire as the four-letter
string `undefined`. REQ-002 pins this for the redirect path; the same invariant is the
reason REQ-007 insists `req.hostname` never returns `undefined` for a syntactically present
host.

**Trust boundary and header re-derivation.** Every `X-Forwarded-*` derivation (REQ-006,
REQ-007) is a trust-boundary crossing gated by one compiled predicate. The invariant is
that trust is decided once, by the function `compileTrust` produced (REQ-008), and that
every getter behind that gate applies the *same* parsing discipline to the
comma-separated header it reads. Differing split/trim behavior between two getters behind
one trust gate is a cross-cutting defect, not a local one — which is why REQ-007 is
tagged as a parity requirement rather than split into three independent getter REQs.

**Header composition is single-writer.** `Content-Type` and its charset are written by
several helpers (REQ-003, REQ-005) and `Set-Cookie` directives by one (REQ-001). The
cross-cutting rule is that whichever helper writes a header writes all of it, coherently:
two mechanisms that both inject a charset must produce the same charset for the same input
(REQ-005), and two directives that both encode a lifetime must encode the same lifetime
(REQ-001).

**Fail at configuration time, not at request time.** REQ-008 states this directly for
`app.set`, but it is the framework's general posture: the setting compilers run eagerly so
that a typo in `trust proxy` is a boot-time `TypeError` rather than a per-request
mis-derivation of `req.ip`. Errors that can be detected without a request should not wait
for one.

**Content negotiation is advisory, serialization is binding.** Parsing an `Accept` header
(REQ-004) informs a choice; writing a `Content-Type` (REQ-005) commits to it. A lenient
parser is acceptable where a lenient serializer is not — this asymmetry is why REQ-004 is
scoped to "do not silently drop or mis-split valid input" while REQ-005 demands exact
agreement between surfaces.

## Use cases

Traceability is one-way REQ → UC; the reverse index is derived in the appendix below. Each
use case renders its actor, trigger, and expected outcome. No use case carries a formal
document reference — this is a Tier 3 run with no citable sources.

### UC-01: Reverse-proxy operator relies on `req.protocol`/`req.secure`
- Actor: backend developer behind a TLS-terminating proxy
- Trigger: a request arrives with `X-Forwarded-Proto`
- Expected outcome: `req.secure` correctly reflects HTTPS so HTTPS-only middleware behaves.

### UC-02: Developer sets a short-lived cookie
- Actor: app developer setting a flash/CSRF cookie with `maxAge`
- Trigger: `res.cookie(name, val, {maxAge})`
- Expected outcome: the cookie lives for the requested duration, not expiring instantly.

### UC-03: API returns a redirect with a custom status
- Actor: API author issuing `res.redirect(status, url)`
- Trigger: a 3xx status outside the common set
- Expected outcome: a clean, human-readable redirect body — never the literal `undefined`.

### UC-04: Client consumes a JSONP endpoint
- Actor: legacy browser client passing `?callback=`
- Trigger: `res.jsonp(obj)`
- Expected outcome: a safe `text/javascript` payload invoking only a validly-named callback.

### UC-05: Client negotiates content with quality params
- Actor: HTTP client sending `Accept` with `q=` and media-type params
- Trigger: `req.accepts` / `res.format`
- Expected outcome: parameters (including quoted values) parsed per RFC 7231.

### UC-06.a: String body with a pre-set charset
- Actor: developer calling `res.set('Content-Type', 'text/plain; charset=iso-8859-1').send('é')`
- Expected outcome: documented, consistent charset behavior for string bodies.

### UC-06.b: Buffer body with a pre-set charset
- Actor: developer sending `Buffer.from('é','latin1')` with a latin1 Content-Type
- Expected outcome: charset behavior consistent with the string-body rule, or explicitly specified divergence.

### UC-06.c: Charset set via `res.set`/`res.type` then `send`
- Actor: developer setting the type via `res.type('html')` then `res.send`
- Expected outcome: `mime.contentType` injection and `setCharset` injection agree.

### UC-07.a: Trusted `X-Forwarded-Host` with a normal authority
- Actor: app behind a trusted proxy
- Expected outcome: `req.hostname`/`req.subdomains` resolve correctly.

### UC-07.b: Trusted `X-Forwarded-Host` with a leading/trailing comma
- Actor: app behind a proxy that concatenates forwarded hosts
- Expected outcome: hostname resolution never silently returns `undefined` for a present host.

### UC-07.c: `X-Forwarded-Host` carrying a port or IPv6 literal
- Actor: app behind a proxy forwarding `host:port` or `[::1]:port`
- Expected outcome: the port is stripped to a clean hostname.
